text.p: Switzerland's Novartis AG said on Tuesday that it expected sales of its anti-rheumatic drug Voltaren to stabilise, despite the impact of generic competition.
Sales of Voltaren, its second biggest-selling product, fell eight percent last year to 1.437 billion Swiss francs as generic competition in the U.S. kicked in.

In an interview with Reuters, Novartis president Daniel Vasella said sales of Voltaren in the first two months of 1997 had stabilized, helped by the addition of Cataflam, a faster-acting form of Voltaren, and of a slow-release formulation of the drug.
"The benefit is that in the first two months we have stability, no further decline," said Vasella, adding "I expect you will see more stability now for a while."
He said the company had also been able to make up some of the decline in sales through its own generic version, although this carried "a much lower margin."

The group's top-selling drug, organ transplant and immune system treatment Neoral/Sandimmun, saw sales rise 10 percent to 1.612 billion Swiss francs last year. However, analysts said this will come under pressure from SangStat Medical Corp's Cyclosporine in 1997.
Novartis estimated that some 20 to 25 percent of its drug sales last year, which totaled 12.18 billion Swiss francs, came from products launched in the past five years.
"The big growth drivers in absolute terms are already on the market," said Vasella.

He singled out anti-fungal treatment Lamisil, whose sales jumped 50 percent to 558 million francs, cholesterol-lowering agent Lescol, whose sales rose 79 percent to 460 million francs, and anti-hypertensive Cibacen/Lotensin, which had sales of 453 million francs, up 37 percent.
Vasella also underlined the importance of heart drug Diovan, which is currently being laucnhed, and Alzheimer's drug Exelon.
"I think these will be very important growth drivers in the future," Vasella added.
